provenance: 24 balanced, manually authored and source-checked claim/evidence pairs based on Ada's public-only FlashAttention-3 run. Evidence is paraphrased from the paper and author blog. This narrow benchmark evaluates claim-verdict behavior, not end-to-end research quality.

sources.title: FlashAttention-3: Fast and Accurate Attention with Asynchrony and Low-precision (paper)

model_verdicts.reason: Evidence explicitly mentions using Tensor Core and TMA asynchrony to overlap computation and data movement.
Evidence directly states interleaving block-wise matrix multiplication and softmax operations.
Evidence reports up to 740 TFLOPs/s and 75% utilization for FP16 on H100.
Evidence reports FP8 performance close to 1.2 PFLOPs/s.
Evidence gives speedups of 1.5x‑2.0x over FlashAttention‑2 for FP16 on H100.
Evidence notes 2.6× lower numerical error for FP8 compared to a baseline implementation.
Evidence states FlashAttention‑2 reached 35% utilization on H100.
Evidence lists block quantization and incoherent processing as techniques for FP8 hardware support.
Evidence supports a 1.5x‑2.0x speedup for attention on H100 with FP16 versus FlashAttention‑2, not for every Transformer workload.
Evidence shows a 2.6× lower numerical error for FP8 only; no FP16 error reduction is reported.
Evidence reports up to 75% utilization on the H100 GPU for FP16, not on all Hopper GPUs.
Evidence lists multiple techniques (asynchrony, interleaving, low‑precision), indicating performance gains are not due solely to asynchrony.
Evidence states performance up to 740 TFLOPs/s on H100, not exactly that value for every H100 configuration.
Evidence compares FP8 to a baseline FP8 implementation; it does not compare FP8 to FP16 accuracy.
Evidence only provides results for Hopper H100, with no data on other GPU architectures.
Evidence concerns attention‑level speedup versus FlashAttention‑2 on H100, not end‑to‑end LLM serving latency.
Evidence states 740 TFLOPs/s is achieved with FP16, not FP8.
Evidence indicates the ~1.2 PFLOPs/s result is for FP8, while FP16 reaches up to 740 TFLOPs/s.
Evidence reports a speedup of 1.5x‑2.0x over FlashAttention‑2, not 10x.
Evidence shows FlashAttention‑2 had 35% utilization, FlashAttention‑3 up to 75%.
Evidence says numerical error is 2.6x lower than baseline FP8, not higher.
Evidence specifies the 740 TFLOPs/s FP16 result was measured on H100, not A100.
Evidence describes use of asynchronous Tensor Core and TMA to overlap computation and data movement.
Evidence attributes ~1.2 PFLOPs/s to FP8, while FP16 reaches up to 740 TFLOPs/s.

limitations: This narrow single-topic benchmark measures claim-verdict behavior, not end-to-end research quality or general-domain accuracy.
Claim-support judgments are model outputs and require human review before being treated as labels.
A missing or invalid verdict is counted as unanswered, not silently dropped.
Langfuse trace delivery is not confirmed unless langfuse_health is healthy.
